summary: Describes how to use RSVP to request the Controlled-Load and Guaranteed quality-of-service controls from the integrated services framework. It defines how the needed parameters are carried in RSVP messages.

plainLanguage.summary: It explains how to fill in the reservation form so the network gives you either a steady, decent connection or one with firm promises.

questions: how to use rsvp with integrated services
what is guaranteed service in rsvp
what is a break bit in rsvp
subtitle: How RSVP carries the traffic, path and reservation data for Controlled-Load and Guaranteed service.

tldr.problem: RSVP treats the objects that invoke quality-of-service controls as opaque, and the Controlled-Load and Guaranteed services need a defined way to carry their parameters.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the contents of the SENDER_TSPEC, ADSPEC and FLOWSPEC objects, using a three-level encoding of message header, per-service fragments and parameters, with break bits to flag hops lacking a service.
tldr.outcome: Senders describe their traffic, the network accumulates path properties for receivers, and receivers choose a service and send a reservation request back upstream.

today: RFC 2210 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines how RSVP from RFC 2205 carries the Controlled-Load and Guaranteed service data.

sections.title: Where This Fits
sections.content:
The integrated services framework lets applications choose among controlled levels of delivery service. It needs two things: network elements that can control quality of service, and a way to communicate requirements along the path. The first is provided by services such as Controlled-Load (RFC 2211) and Guaranteed (RFC 2212). The second is frequently provided by a setup protocol such as RSVP (RFC 2205).

RSVP treats the objects related to QoS services as opaque. This RFC defines the usage and contents of three of them, FLOWSPEC, ADSPEC and SENDER_TSPEC, for an environment supporting Controlled-Load and/or Guaranteed service.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP is the delivery truck, and this RFC says what to write on the forms inside it.

sections.title: Three Objects, Two Directions
sections.content:
Each object carries a different kind of data.

  • SENDER_TSPEC carries the Sender TSpec, a description of the traffic a sender will generate. It travels downstream and is never modified inside the network.
  • ADSPEC carries information produced at senders or network elements, such as available services and delay and bandwidth estimates. It flows downstream and is updated at each hop, summarised so its size stays roughly constant.
  • FLOWSPEC carries the receiver's reservation request: the desired service, a TSpec and, if the service needs one, an RSpec. It flows upstream toward senders.

The RFC notes that having both SENDER_TSPEC and ADSPEC is somewhat historical, but the split between data that is and is not updated in the network may be useful in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender fills in how much it will send. The network adds notes on the way. The receiver sends back the order.

sections.title: How a Reservation Is Set Up
sections.content:
A sending application registers with RSVP, giving its Sender TSpec. That goes into a SENDER_TSPEC object in the PATH messages. The sender also builds an initial ADSPEC. At each network element the ADSPEC goes to the traffic control module, which asks each mentioned service to update its part. If a service in the ADSPEC is not implemented, a flag is set for the receiver.

At the receiver, the SENDER_TSPEC and ADSPEC are passed to the application, which picks reservation parameters: the service (Guaranteed or Controlled-Load), the TSpec and, if needed, an RSpec. RSVP sends these upstream as a FLOWSPEC. At each RSVP-aware point the arriving SENDER_TSPECs and FLOWSPECs are used to request a reservation from the chosen service. Finally the merged FLOWSPEC reaches each sender.

In RSVP version 1, all receivers in a session must choose the same QoS control service. A sender can steer this by omitting the ADSPEC fragment of a service it does not want used.
sections.plainLanguage: The message goes from sender to receiver collecting notes, and the order goes back the other way.

sections.title: Break Bits and Path MTU
sections.content:
The ADSPEC carries break bits that show whether a fully reservation-capable path exists. The break bit in service 1's header (the global one) is set when some element does not support RSVP and integrated services at all; then the other ADSPEC values are unreliable. A service-specific break bit means an element supports RSVP but not that service.

The RFC also describes MTU negotiation. Senders put their largest packet size in the M field of the TSpec. The ADSPEC carries a PATH_MTU parameter, which gives the minimum MTU along the path. Each receiver takes the minimum across senders and uses it as M in its request. At merge points the smaller M is forwarded upstream, and packets larger than the final value may be delivered as best effort rather than covered by the reservation.
sections.plainLanguage: If one road on the route cannot carry a special lane, a flag goes up. Everyone also learns the smallest truck that fits through every road.

sections.title: Object Formats
sections.content:
The SENDER_TSPEC carries a Token_Bucket_TSpec (service 1, parameter 127) with token bucket rate r, bucket size b, peak rate p, minimum policed unit m and maximum packet size M. A value of zero for m is illegal.

The FLOWSPEC uses the same TSpec. A service header value of 5 requests Controlled-Load, and 2 requests Guaranteed. Guaranteed also adds an RSpec (parameter 130) with a rate R and a slack term S.

The ADSPEC starts with a message header and a fragment for the default general parameters (service 1), followed by optional Guaranteed (2) and Controlled-Load (5) fragments, always in service number order. The Guaranteed fragment carries the composed Ctot, Dtot, Csum and Dsum values. The Controlled-Load fragment normally has no extra data. A service fragment may also carry override parameters that replace global values with service-specific ones.
sections.plainLanguage: Each form has fixed boxes: how fast, how big a burst, how big a packet. The special-promise form has two extra boxes.

sections.title: The Three-Level Encoding
sections.content:
Appendix 1 gives a general wire format. A 32-bit message header holds a version (currently 0) and a length in 32-bit words, not counting the header word. Each per-service header has a service number, the break bit and a length. Each parameter header has a parameter number, flags and a length, followed by the data. Parameter values are encoded with XDR (RFC 1832).

Length fields exclude their own header word, so an element that does not know a service can set its break bit and skip over the fragment.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is a set of boxes inside boxes, each labelled with its size, so anyone can skip a box they do not understand.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The message formatting and usage rules raise no security issues of their own. Using them to offer several qualities of service creates a new requirement: controlling and authenticating access to enhanced service. That is discussed in RFC 2205, RFC 2212 and RFC 2211. A separate document on RSVP cryptographic authentication, a work in progress at the time, describes protecting the integrity of the messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The forms themselves are safe, but someone must check who is allowed to ask for the special lane.
